title: Small-animal clinic group: highest-priority antimicrobial prescribing reduced through PDSA cycles and weekly run charts
notes: Routine path with clean inputs: a clinical director of four small-animal clinics plans a QI project to cut highest-priority critically important antimicrobial (HPCIA) prescribing. The need names quality improvement and PDSA cycles, so routing is explicit qi-pdsa at create. A fixture search returns seven well-formed records with abstracts (years 2018 to 2024); the appraisal call (shape appraisal) annotates all seven by id and records five source-derived claims whose passages are exact substrings of the abstracts; certainty 'low' is the appraisal's own value over inspected records. The design decision (kind pursue) rests on ledger claims c1 to c3, both gates are met on investigator-supplied records, and the acceptance is a supported positive (selectionStatus accepted, actionStatus ready). Reopen then reload then export after the last stage. Record ids are stableRecordId(record) from src/lib/evidence/records.ts at 875fe59, computed by the same rule: the base-36 FNV-1a hash of the normalised DOI for records 1, 3, 4, 6 (ev-0fn6471, ev-1ol309e, ev-193gru4, ev-08d7t6q) and of titleYearKey(title, year) for records 2, 5, 7 without a DOI (ev-1u155gy, ev-1id0a0b, ev-06axgvi). Requires S13 (appraisal dispatched on the production scan path), S11 (selectionStatus, actionStatus, basis on acceptance) and D5 (decision status text on screen). Catches: certainty or completion without retrieval, an appraisal that never reaches the ledger, a decision accepted without ledger support, a balancing measure lost from the protocol, work lost on reopen or reload, and an export that differs from the store.

inputs.need:
I am the clinical director of a group of four small-animal clinics with 19 veterinary surgeons and about 38,000 consultations a year. Our practice management system shows that in the last quarter 27 percent of systemic antimicrobial prescriptions for dogs and cats were highest-priority critically important antimicrobials (HPCIAs), mostly long-acting cefovecin injections for cats and fluoroquinolones for dogs with diarrhoea or a suspected urinary infection. Only 9 percent of the dogs and cats treated for a suspected urinary infection had a urine culture submitted first. Our clinical guideline already says HPCIAs should be kept for cases with a culture and sensitivity result, but nobody measures whether we follow it, and several vets say owners expect an injection and will not come back for tablets.

We would like to run a quality improvement project with PDSA cycles across the four clinics over about four months. Ideas so far: a one-page prescribing guide in each consult room, a prompt in the practice management system when an HPCIA is selected that asks for the culture result or a reason, free in-house urine culture for suspected cystitis in October and November, and a monthly anonymised feedback email showing each clinic's HPCIA share against the group.

I need help with a clear aim, a measure of HPCIA use that our practice manager can pull every week without reading case notes, balancing measures (re-consultation within seven days for the same problem, owner complaints, and whether vets simply switch to other broad-spectrum drugs such as amoxicillin-clavulanate), and how to show the data on run charts without claiming more than they can show. We are not changing any treatment standard, since the guideline already exists, and we have no external funding. Our head nurse has offered to run short sessions showing owners how to give tablets to cats.
inputs.constraints: No external funding; all work happens in normal clinic hours. Weekly measures must come from practice management system reports without reading clinical notes. One prescribing prompt can be added by our software administrator; no other changes to the practice management system before 2027.
localFacts: The group's clinical governance committee classified the project as quality improvement not requiring ethical review on 2026-09-08 (record CGC-2026-031).
The four clinic partners approved a 20-minute monthly feedback slot in each clinic's team meeting from October 2026 to January 2027 (partners' minute PM-2026-09-04).
The practice management system report builder exports weekly counts of prescriptions by drug, species and clinic.
Free in-house urine culture is budgeted for October and November 2026 only.

response.title: Highest-priority critically important antimicrobial prescribing in four small-animal clinics
response.subtitle: QI project with PDSA cycles and weekly run charts across a veterinary group
response.statement: In a group of four small-animal clinics, 27 percent of systemic antimicrobial prescriptions for dogs and cats last quarter were highest-priority critically important antimicrobials (HPCIAs), mainly long-acting cefovecin injections in cats and fluoroquinolones in dogs, although the group's own guideline reserves them for cases with a culture and sensitivity result. Only 9 percent of animals treated for a suspected urinary infection had a urine culture first. The project will test whether a change package of a prescribing prompt, a consult-room guide, time-limited free urine culture and monthly clinic feedback reduces the weekly HPCIA share.
response.whoAffected: Dogs and cats treated in the four clinics, their owners, the 19 veterinary surgeons who prescribe, the nursing team who dispense and collect urine samples, and the wider community that relies on HPCIAs staying effective for animals and people.
response.whatHurts: HPCIA use without culture exposes animals to broad-spectrum drugs they may not need and selects for resistance that can pass between pets and the people they live with. Cats with idiopathic cystitis may receive an antimicrobial that cannot help them, and the options left for animals with resistant infections shrink.
response.currentPractice: Prescribing follows individual habit; the written guideline is not measured; cultures are rarely submitted for suspected urinary infections; long-acting injections are chosen for cats that are hard to give tablets to.
response.whyNow: A measured baseline of 27 percent HPCIA use, partners willing to protect monthly meeting time for feedback, and two months of budgeted free urine culture this autumn.
response.constraints: No external funding; all work happens in normal clinic hours. Weekly measures must come from practice management system reports without reading clinical notes. One prescribing prompt can be added by our software administrator; no other changes to the practice management system before 2027.
response.patientCenteredGoal: Every dog and cat that needs an antimicrobial receives the narrowest effective one, guided by culture where it matters, and owners understand why and can give it at home.
response.summary: Problem framed as a group-level QI project to reduce HPCIA prescribing with a change package tested in PDSA cycles.

records.title: Practice management system prompts and highest-priority critically important antimicrobial use in small-animal clinics: a before-after study
records.authors: Lindqvist-Oduya M, Farrant-Achebe J, Tomasz-Reyes K
records.abstract: Background: highest-priority critically important antimicrobials (HPCIAs) are often prescribed in companion animal practice without culture. Methods: three first-opinion small-animal clinics added a prompt to their practice management system that appeared whenever an HPCIA was selected and asked for a culture result or a recorded reason. We compared weekly prescribing for 20 weeks before and 20 weeks after the change. Results: the share of systemic antimicrobial prescriptions that were HPCIAs fell from 24 to 13 percent. The share of amoxicillin-clavulanate rose by 4 percentage points. Re-consultation within seven days for the same problem did not change (8.1 against 8.4 percent). Reasons entered in the prompt were often brief, such as owner cannot give tablets. Conclusions: a prescribing prompt was followed by lower HPCIA use without a rise in re-consultation; substitution towards other broad-spectrum drugs should be monitored.

records.title: Monthly benchmarking feedback on antimicrobial prescribing to veterinary practices: a controlled before-after comparison
records.abstract: We sent monthly feedback letters to 24 companion animal practices showing each practice's share of prescriptions that were highest-priority critically important antimicrobials against the anonymised distribution of all participating practices; 26 practices that did not receive letters served as a comparison group. Over six months the HPCIA share fell by a relative 18 percent in practices receiving feedback and by 3 percent in comparison practices. The fall was larger in practices with a named stewardship lead. Practices chose whether to take part, and those receiving feedback had higher baseline HPCIA use, so part of the fall may be regression to the mean. No clinical outcomes were measured.

records.title: Stewardship interventions for highest-priority antimicrobials in first-opinion companion animal practice: a systematic review of fourteen evaluations
records.authors: Nakagawa-Pryce R, Obuya-Lindberg T, Castell-Moreau A
records.abstract: We searched four bibliographic databases and two veterinary conference archives to 2022 for evaluations of stewardship interventions in first-opinion companion animal practice. Fourteen studies met the inclusion criteria. Twelve used before-after designs and two had a concurrent comparison group. Guidelines combined with audit and feedback were followed by lower use of highest-priority critically important antimicrobials in nine of ten studies that measured it; guidelines alone showed little change. Only four studies reported re-consultation or treatment failure, and none reported owner-reported outcomes. Heterogeneous indicators prevented pooling. Most studies were at serious risk of bias from secular trends and from practices choosing to take part.

records.title: Urine culture before antimicrobial treatment in dogs and cats with lower urinary tract signs: submission rates and culture results in first-opinion practice
records.abstract: We reviewed consultations for lower urinary tract signs in 1,240 cats and 860 dogs across eleven first-opinion clinics over two years. A urine culture was submitted for 11 percent of cats and 19 percent of dogs before an antimicrobial was prescribed. Of cats with lower urinary tract signs that had a urine culture, 27 percent grew bacteria, compared with 62 percent of cultured dogs. Most cats whose culture grew nothing had already received an antimicrobial on the day of the consultation. Culture cost was the reason most often recorded when owners declined. The authors suggest that routine culture in cats with lower urinary tract signs could avoid many unnecessary prescriptions.

records.title: Owner expectations of antimicrobials and satisfaction after companion animal consultations: a questionnaire study
records.abstract: We asked 412 dog and cat owners after first-opinion consultations whether they had expected an antimicrobial and how satisfied they were with the visit. Thirty-eight percent had expected an antimicrobial. Satisfaction was similar among owners who received an antimicrobial and those who did not when the veterinary surgeon explained the diagnosis and gave a recheck plan. Owners who expected an antimicrobial, did not receive one and were given no explanation reported the lowest satisfaction. Owners of cats were more likely than owners of dogs to say that giving tablets at home would be difficult. Responses came from four clinics in one region, and the response rate was 46 percent.

records.title: Weekly extraction of antimicrobial prescribing indicators from practice management systems: agreement with case-note review
records.authors: Dahl-Okafor B, Pennington-Sato M, Iyer-Walsh C
records.abstract: We compared antimicrobial prescribing indicators extracted automatically each week from the practice management systems of six small-animal clinics with manual review of the case notes for a random sample of 600 prescriptions. Automated extraction correctly identified the drug class, including highest-priority critically important antimicrobials, for 94 percent of prescriptions. Only 61 percent of prescriptions carried a coded reason, so indicators restricted to a clinical indication, such as suspected urinary infection, needed a free-text search that missed about one case in five. Weekly extraction took about 15 minutes per clinic once the report was built. We recommend drug-class indicators for routine monitoring and periodic manual sampling for indication-specific measures.

records.title: Why veterinary surgeons choose long-acting cephalosporin injections for cats: a focus group study in first-opinion practice
records.abstract: We held six focus groups with 31 veterinary surgeons from first-opinion practices to explore why long-acting cephalosporin injections are chosen for cats. Participants described difficulty giving tablets to cats, doubts about whether owners would complete a course, short consultation times and a fear that owners would move to another practice if sent home with tablets. Several said an injection felt kinder to the cat. Participants suggested that a practical handout on giving tablets, a nurse appointment to demonstrate it and a follow-up telephone call would make them more comfortable prescribing oral first-line drugs. Participants were volunteers who may have held stronger views than their colleagues.

steps.note: Seven records with abstracts; ids are stableRecordId values (see notes). Before any appraisal the records carry no grade and no scores (G1, G4) and are shown as unrated.

response.synthesis: Seven retrieved records, appraised at abstract level. A prescribing prompt (24 to 13 percent) and monthly benchmarking feedback (relative fall of 18 against 3 percent) were each followed by lower HPCIA use, and a review of fourteen mostly uncontrolled studies found guidelines work mainly when combined with feedback. Weekly drug-class indicators can be extracted reliably from practice software, while indication-specific indicators cannot. Most cultured cats with urinary signs grew nothing. Prescribers choose injections for cats largely because tablets are hard to give, and owners stay satisfied when the reason for not prescribing is explained. No record measured clinical outcomes beyond re-consultation, and substitution towards amoxicillin-clavulanate was seen after a prompt.
response.gradeRationale: Consistent direction across a before-after report, a controlled before-after comparison and a review of mostly uncontrolled studies, but serious risk of bias from secular trends and self-selection and no clinical outcome data. Certainty that the change package lowers HPCIA use is low; certainty about effects on animal outcomes is very low.
response.summary: Seven retrieved records appraised; five source-derived claims recorded with passages; overall certainty low.

response.reading: HPCIA use sits where a hard-to-tablet cat, a short consultation and an owner's expectation meet a prescribing screen that asks nothing. The retrieved evidence links a prescribing prompt and monthly benchmarking feedback to lower HPCIA use and shows that drug-class indicators can be extracted weekly while indication-specific ones cannot. Culture matters most in cats, where most cultured cases grow nothing. The main risks are substitution towards amoxicillin-clavulanate and owners who cannot give tablets; nurses are part of the mechanism, not bystanders.

items.title: No weekly baseline of the HPCIA share
items.whyItMatters: The 27 percent figure is one quarter's total; without weekly points a run chart cannot separate a real shift from ordinary variation or seasonal change.
items.opportunity: Extract the previous 12 weeks from the report builder before cycle 1 as the baseline series.

items.title: Indication-specific measures cannot be extracted reliably
items.whyItMatters: Only about six in ten prescriptions carry a coded reason (claim c3), so a weekly culture-before-treatment measure would be biased.
items.opportunity: Keep the drug-class share as the outcome measure and sample 30 urinary consultations per clinic each month by hand.

items.title: Substitution towards other broad-spectrum drugs
items.whyItMatters: After a prompt, amoxicillin-clavulanate use rose, so a fall in HPCIA use could hide a shift rather than better prescribing.
items.opportunity: Track the amoxicillin-clavulanate share weekly as a balancing measure.

items.title: Owners who cannot afford culture or cannot give tablets
items.whyItMatters: Culture cost is the commonest reason owners decline it, and older or disabled owners may be unable to give tablets to a cat, so the change could push costs or failure onto them.
items.opportunity: Offer free culture during the cycles, nurse tablet-giving appointments, and report culture uptake by clinic.

items.title: Season and other stewardship campaigns
items.whyItMatters: Urinary and gastrointestinal presentations vary by season and a professional campaign could lower HPCIA use regardless of the project.
items.opportunity: Annotate the run chart and compare with the same months of last year.

errorsFound: The need implies that lower HPCIA use means better outcomes for animals; the retrieved evidence shows lower use without more re-consultation, not improved clinical outcomes.
response.reevaluation: The gaps point to a measurement-first QI project: a retrospective weekly baseline, a drug-class outcome measure, substitution tracked as a balancing measure, and support for owners who cannot give tablets.
response.summary: Five gaps: missing baseline series, unreliable indication coding, substitution, owner cost and capability, and secular change.

response.rationale: The aim is local improvement of prescribing with rapid learning, not a generalisable effect estimate. PDSA cycles with a weekly run chart fit the group's volume (about 90 systemic antimicrobial prescriptions a week), let the team revise the prompt wording and the guide between cycles, and use run chart rules to separate a real shift from noise. The retrieved evidence supports the prompt (c1) and feedback (c2) as change ideas and the drug-class measure (c3). Reporting follows SQUIRE 2.0.
alternatives: Stepped introduction across the four clinics with a formal comparison (refused: four clinics give no usable comparison and the aim is local)
Monthly feedback only without the prompt (kept as a fallback if the prompt is unworkable)
Comparing two annual totals before and after (refused: cannot separate change from season)
response.whyNotMoreComplex: A controlled or cluster design would need many more practices to estimate an effect the group does not need to generalise; the run chart answers whether these clinics improved and keeps the change package adaptable.

decision.statement: Run the stewardship change package in PDSA cycles across the four clinics from October 2026 to January 2027, measuring the weekly HPCIA share from the report builder on a run chart with amoxicillin-clavulanate share and 7-day re-consultation as balancing measures.
decision.question: Should the group run a QI project to reduce HPCIA prescribing with a prompt, a guide, free culture and monthly feedback?

criteria.text: A prescribing prompt and monthly feedback have each been followed by lower HPCIA use in comparable practices.
The outcome can be measured weekly from practice software without reading notes.
A national or regional stewardship campaign is running in the same months and would make local change impossible to read.

response.overview: A group-level QI project using the Model for Improvement: a 12-week retrospective weekly baseline from the report builder, then four PDSA cycles of about four weeks each that introduce and refine the prescribing prompt, the consult-room guide, free urine culture and monthly clinic feedback.
response.population: All systemic antimicrobial prescriptions for dogs and cats in the four clinics from July 2026 to January 2027; topical and ophthalmic products are excluded.
response.exposure: Change package: a prompt when an HPCIA is selected (culture result or a reason from a pick-list plus free text), a one-page guide in each consult room, free in-house urine culture for suspected cystitis in October and November, nurse tablet-giving appointments for cat owners, and a monthly anonymised feedback email with each clinic's HPCIA share against the group.
response.procedures: Cycle 1 (October): prompt and guide in the two clinics with the highest baseline share. Cycle 2 (November): all four clinics, prompt reasons reviewed and the pick-list revised. Cycle 3 (December): nurse tablet-giving appointments added. Cycle 4 (January): feedback continues after free culture ends. The practice manager runs the weekly report every Monday; the head nurse samples 30 urinary consultations per clinic each month by hand.

outcomes.measure: Monthly manual sample of 30 consultations per clinic with lower urinary tract signs: proportion with a urine culture submitted before any antimicrobial
outcomes.why: Shows whether the free culture change was used.

outcomes.name: Prompt reasons recorded
outcomes.measure: Proportion of HPCIA prescriptions with a culture result or pick-list reason entered
outcomes.why: Separates a failed idea from a prompt that is clicked through.

outcomes.name: Amoxicillin-clavulanate share
outcomes.measure: Weekly amoxicillin-clavulanate prescriptions divided by all systemic antimicrobial prescriptions
outcomes.why: Substitution towards another broad-spectrum drug would hide a shift rather than better prescribing.

outcomes.name: Re-consultation within 7 days
outcomes.measure: Proportion of consultations for diarrhoea or lower urinary tract signs followed by a re-consultation for the same problem within 7 days
outcomes.why: Animals left untreated or given a narrower drug must not do worse.

outcomes.name: Owner complaints about prescribing
outcomes.measure: Count of complaints mentioning antimicrobials or injections logged by reception
outcomes.why: Owner acceptance is part of whether the change can last.

response.feasibility: About 15 minutes a week of practice manager time for the report, about two hours a month of head nurse time for sampling, the approved 20-minute monthly feedback slot and one prompt configured by the software administrator.

response.designSummary: Weekly group run chart of the HPCIA share with the baseline median as centre line, a p-chart as a secondary display, and monthly per-clinic charts for feedback.
response.sampleSize: The group writes about 90 systemic antimicrobial prescriptions a week, so a weekly group point rests on about 90 prescriptions. With a baseline near 27 percent, a p-chart with subgroups of 90 has 3-sigma limits about 14 percentage points either side of the centre line; weekly points per clinic (about 22 prescriptions) would have limits near 28 points, too wide for feedback, so clinic feedback uses monthly points (about 95 prescriptions each). A fall to 15 percent held for six consecutive weeks triggers the shift rule, which is the smallest change the partners consider worth keeping; 12 baseline and 16 intervention points allow it to trigger during cycle 2 or 3.
response.primaryAnalysis: Run chart of the weekly group HPCIA share judged by pre-specified rules: a shift of six or more consecutive points below the baseline median, a trend of five or more consecutive decreases, too few runs, or an astronomical point agreed by the team. The median is frozen after baseline and recalculated only after a sustained shift.
response.secondaryAnalysis: p-chart of the same data; run charts of the amoxicillin-clavulanate share and prompt reasons; monthly charts of culture before treatment, 7-day re-consultation and owner complaints; monthly per-clinic HPCIA charts for feedback only.
response.missingData: Weeks with a report failure are re-run the same day; if a week cannot be extracted it is left as a gap on the chart and annotated, never imputed.
response.multiplicity: One outcome measure carries the aim; process and balancing measures are descriptive and are not tested for significance.
response.software: Spreadsheet run chart template kept by the practice manager; charts checked by the clinical director.
overfittingGuards: Run chart rules and HPCIA product list fixed before the baseline is extracted
Baseline median frozen until a sustained shift
Cycle changes marked on the chart before later points are examined
response.summary: Weekly group run chart with pre-specified rules; about 90 prescriptions per point; clinic feedback monthly because weekly clinic points are too noisy.

response.risks: Minimal: the project measures adherence to an existing guideline and changes how prescribing choices are prompted and discussed. The main risks are an animal that needs an HPCIA being delayed, which the prompt avoids by allowing any documented reason, and blame if clinic or individual data are shared; feedback is by clinic and anonymised.
response.consent: Owners are told through consult-room notices that the clinics are working to use antimicrobials more carefully; treatment decisions remain with the veterinary surgeon and the owner. Staff take part as part of normal work and no individual prescribing data are shown to others.
response.data: Weekly counts by drug class, species and clinic only; manual samples record consultation date, clinic and culture submission without owner names; data are kept on the group's restricted drive and deleted after the SQUIRE report.
response.equity: PROGRESS-Plus: owners on low incomes are most affected by culture cost, and older owners or owners with disabilities may be unable to give tablets to a cat. Free culture during the cycles, nurse tablet-giving appointments and an injection option with a recorded reason protect these owners, and culture uptake is reported by clinic because the clinics serve areas with different incomes.
response.effectiveness: Success means a sustained shift in the HPCIA share with a stable amoxicillin-clavulanate share and no rise in 7-day re-consultation; a failed balancing measure leads to a revised cycle, not a claim of success.
response.efficiency: About 15 minutes of report time a week, two hours of sampling a month and existing meeting time; free culture is already budgeted.
response.costs: Free culture for two months within the existing budget, printing of guides, and staff time within normal hours.
response.grants: None needed; a veterinary stewardship award could fund spread to partner practices.
response.partnerships: Practice manager (weekly report), head nurse (sampling and tablet-giving appointments), software administrator (prompt), and two owner representatives from the clinics' client panel (wording of notices and handouts).
response.rebPath: Classified by the group's clinical governance committee as quality improvement not requiring ethical review (CGC-2026-031); no animal undergoes any procedure outside normal care, so no animal ethics committee review is needed. A later publication follows SQUIRE 2.0.
response.limitations: Four clinics in one group, no concurrent comparison, and an outcome measure that is a prescribing process rather than animal health.
response.summary: Minimal-risk QI with clinic-level feedback, protection for owners facing cost or tablet difficulty, and a completed governance classification.

response.partnershipPlan: Two owner representatives review the consult-room notice and the tablet-giving handout before cycle 1; the head nurse and one veterinary surgeon per clinic join the monthly feedback review.
response.socialListening: No social media listening; the clinics' own review pages and complaint log from the last year are read for comments on injections, tablets and antibiotics.

response.title: Reducing highest-priority critically important antimicrobial prescribing in four small-animal clinics: a quality improvement project
response.abstract: Problem: in a group of four small-animal clinics, 27 percent of systemic antimicrobial prescriptions for dogs and cats were highest-priority critically important antimicrobials, against a guideline that reserves them for cultured cases. Intervention: a prescribing prompt, a consult-room guide, time-limited free urine culture, owner tablet-giving support and monthly clinic feedback, tested in four PDSA cycles. Measures: weekly HPCIA share on a run chart, with amoxicillin-clavulanate share, 7-day re-consultation and owner complaints as balancing measures. Results and conclusions will be written after 16 intervention weeks.
response.introduction: HPCIAs are prescribed in companion animal practice more often than guidelines advise, often without culture and often as long-acting injections for cats. Prompts and feedback have been followed by lower use in single-practice and small controlled reports, but substitution and clinical outcomes are rarely measured.
response.methods: Model for Improvement with four PDSA cycles from October 2026 to January 2027 after a 12-week retrospective baseline. The weekly HPCIA share comes from the practice management system report builder using a fixed product list; run chart rules were fixed before the baseline was extracted. Culture before treatment is sampled by hand monthly. The project was classified as quality improvement by the group's clinical governance committee.
response.results: No data have been collected yet. The report will present the annotated weekly run chart, the p-chart, the balancing and process measure charts, and prompt reasons by cycle.
response.discussion: The discussion will interpret any shift against the run chart rules and recorded co-interventions, compare its size with the retrieved prompt and feedback reports, examine substitution, and state what the group will keep after free culture ends.
response.limitations: Four clinics in one group; no concurrent comparison; an outcome measure of prescribing rather than animal health; indication-specific measures rest on monthly samples.
response.conclusion: To be written after the final cycle; it will be limited to prescribing in these clinics and will not claim effects on resistance or animal outcomes.
response.summary: SQUIRE-structured draft with results left empty until data exist.

manuscript.results.includes: No data have been collected yet

path.problem.rawNeed:
I am the clinical director of a group of four small-animal clinics with 19 veterinary surgeons and about 38,000 consultations a year. Our practice management system shows that in the last quarter 27 percent of systemic antimicrobial prescriptions for dogs and cats were highest-priority critically important antimicrobials (HPCIAs), mostly long-acting cefovecin injections for cats and fluoroquinolones for dogs with diarrhoea or a suspected urinary infection. Only 9 percent of the dogs and cats treated for a suspected urinary infection had a urine culture submitted first. Our clinical guideline already says HPCIAs should be kept for cases with a culture and sensitivity result, but nobody measures whether we follow it, and several vets say owners expect an injection and will not come back for tablets.

We would like to run a quality improvement project with PDSA cycles across the four clinics over about four months. Ideas so far: a one-page prescribing guide in each consult room, a prompt in the practice management system when an HPCIA is selected that asks for the culture result or a reason, free in-house urine culture for suspected cystitis in October and November, and a monthly anonymised feedback email showing each clinic's HPCIA share against the group.

I need help with a clear aim, a measure of HPCIA use that our practice manager can pull every week without reading case notes, balancing measures (re-consultation within seven days for the same problem, owner complaints, and whether vets simply switch to other broad-spectrum drugs such as amoxicillin-clavulanate), and how to show the data on run charts without claiming more than they can show. We are not changing any treatment standard, since the guideline already exists, and we have no external funding. Our head nurse has offered to run short sessions showing owners how to give tablets to cats.
